connection: ClockEntry and ClockEntryService already communicate failure in two ways. This session asks why, fixes one clock-out range-validation bug, and preserves the four contracts with focused tests.
objectives: Distinguish an expected service rejection from an object operation its current state cannot support.
Verify false, InvalidOperationException, and ArgumentOutOfRangeException contracts with deterministic tests.
Pass callable code to Assert.Throws through a lambda and inspect the captured exception.
Recognize that richer service outcomes belong in optional Side Lab 24B.

visuals.title: Expected rejection stays in normal flow
visuals.explanation: No open entry is an ordinary service-level outcome, so TryClockOut returns false and lets its caller branch.

visuals.title: Unsupported object operations throw
visuals.explanation: A completed ClockEntry cannot be completed again, and an open ClockEntry cannot report a completed duration.

visuals.title: Bad argument and bad state are different
visuals.explanation: A clock-out before clock-in makes the incoming argument invalid, so ClockOutEntry reports ArgumentOutOfRangeException rather than InvalidOperationException.

visuals.title: Tests preserve each public contract
visuals.explanation: Separate tests prove the expected false result, both invalid-state exceptions, and the invalid clock-out range.

preQuiz.prompt: What should TryClockOut return when no open entry exists?
preQuiz.explanation: The service treats this as an expected rejection during normal use.

preQuiz.prompt: Why does GetDuration throw while Clockout is null?
options: An open entry has no completed duration
Nullable analysis requires every method to throw
preQuiz.explanation: The object cannot know a finished interval until clock-out occurs.

preQuiz.prompt: What does Assert.Throws need as its second half?
options: The result of running the method first
preQuiz.explanation: A lambda gives xUnit the operation so the assertion can invoke and observe it.

concept.title: Expected rejection versus unsupported operation
paragraphs: All four Session 24 cases can be called invalid in everyday speech. The useful design question is whether the outcome is expected in the normal business workflow or whether the caller is asking an object to perform an operation its current state cannot support.
This is a design convention, not an absolute law. A richer service could replace bool with an enum or Result object; optional Side Lab 24B compares those alternatives.

rows: Allow technical exception to reach centralized handling

concept.title: Inspect what already works before changing it
paragraphs: ClockEntry already rejects duplicate completion with InvalidOperationException and rejects GetDuration while the entry is open. ClockEntryService.TryClockOut already returns false when its repository finds no open entry. The lab inspects these contracts once and then tests them; it does not ask you to reimplement working behavior.
The range guard compares the proposed clockOut parameter with ClockIn. Its exception should name clockOut and explain that clock-out cannot be earlier than clock-in.

concept.title: Assert.Throws needs code it can execute
paragraphs: Calling clockEntry.ClockOutEntry(clockOut) inside the argument list runs it immediately. Because ClockOutEntry returns void, there is no operation left for Assert.Throws to invoke.
The lambda () => clockEntry.ClockOutEntry(clockOut) means: here is code xUnit can run. Assert.Throws commonly accepts an Action—callable code that takes no arguments and returns nothing.
Memory anchor: Method call: run now. Lambda: give xUnit code to run. For a deeper signature-reading exercise using both Enumerable.Join and Assert.Throws<T>, revisit optional Side Lab 01B.

concept.title: Capture the exception to verify the exact rule
paragraphs: Assert.Throws returns the exception object. Store it when the test must inspect Message or ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ParamName.

A message assertion proves the intended rule caused the failure, protects the explanation callers or logs receive, and avoids a test passing because an unrelated exception of the same type occurred. Case-insensitive Contains assertions keep the test focused on meaning rather than capitalization.

lab.objective: Choose how each failure is communicated and preserve that decision with four focused tests.
lab.startingCondition: ClockEntry already rejects duplicate completion and open-entry duration requests. ClockEntryService already returns false when no open entry exists. Inspect those behaviors once; only the range exception and tests require implementation work.
keyPoints: Setup code: you may paste the fixed ClockEntry and DateTime arrangements so test data does not consume the exercise.
Learning code: write each Assert.Throws lambda, choose the expected exception type, capture the exception, and preserve the intended rule with assertions.
Remember: a fixed DateTime keeps a test predictable; false is still a meaningful result; Assert.Throws needs code it can execute.

steps.text: In src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/Models/ClockEntry.cs, inspect ClockEntry.ClockOutEntry and ClockEntry.GetDuration; identify the two existing InvalidOperationException guards without rewriting them.
In src/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain/ClockEntryService.cs, inspect ClockEntryService.TryClockOut and confirm that openClockItem being null returns false.
In ClockEntry.ClockOutEntry, replace the existing clock-out range exception with ArgumentOutOfRangeException that names clockOut and says clock-out cannot be earlier than clock-in.
In ClockOutEntry_WhenAlreadyComplete_ThrowsInvalidOperationException, use fixed DateTime setup values to create and complete one ClockEntry once.

In the same test, write an Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException> lambda that calls ClockOutEntry again, store the exception in error, and assert that error.Message contains already complete without case sensitivity.
In GetDuration_WhenEntryIsOpen_ThrowsInvalidOperationException, create an open ClockEntry with a fixed DateTime and do not call ClockOutEntry.

In that test, pass a lambda calling clockEntry.GetDuration to Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException>, store the exception in error, and assert that its message contains clock out without case sensitivity.

In TryClockOut_WhenNoOpenEntryExists_ReturnsFalse, construct ClockEntryRepository and ClockEntryService, call TryClockOut with a fixed DateTime for an employee with no open entry, and assert that result is false.
Add ClockOutEntry_WhenClockOutPrecedesClockIn_ThrowsArgumentOutOfRangeException and create a ClockEntry whose fixed clockOut value is one minute earlier than ClockIn.

In that range test, capture ArgumentOutOfRangeException through an Assert.Throws lambda, assert that ParamName is clockOut, and assert that Message contains earlier than clock-in without case sensitivity.
Run dotnet test tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj, then compare your work with the hidden solution.

reveals.title: Solution
reveals.text: Reveal only after completing the lab or when you are genuinely blocked.

lab.expectedBehavior: Existing workflows remain unchanged. Four deterministic tests distinguish an expected false result, invalid object state, and an out-of-range argument.
lab.validation: dotnet build PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests/PinkMachine19.TimeClock.Domain.Tests.csproj --configuration Release --no-build && dotnet test PinkMachine19.TimeClock.sln --configuration Release --no-build

expectedFiles.why: Correct the incoming clockOut range exception and message.
Verify the existing false result without rewriting it.
Preserve four failure contracts with focused tests.

commit: session-24: teach validation results and exceptions
review: Existing duplicate-completion, open-duration, and no-open-entry behavior was inspected rather than reimplemented.
Assert.Throws receives a lambda instead of an already-executed void method call.
Fixed DateTime values keep every test deterministic.
Exception messages identify the intended rule.

postQuiz.prompt: Why not make TryClockOut throw when no open entry exists?
options: Its Try name and bool return define an expected rejection contract
Exceptions cannot be used in services
postQuiz.explanation: The current service contract lets callers branch on a normal outcome.

options: It gives xUnit callable code to execute
postQuiz.explanation: Method call means run now; lambda means give xUnit code to run.

postQuiz.prompt: Why store the exception returned by Assert.Throws?
options: To verify its message or parameter name
postQuiz.explanation: The captured object lets the test confirm the intended rule caused the failure.

reflections: Why is no open entry expected at the service boundary but duplicate completion unsupported inside ClockEntry?
What does the lambda delay so Assert.Throws can observe it?
When would a richer enum or Result object communicate more than bool?
whatBreaks: Removing the false guard from TryClockOut misreports an expected rejection. Removing either InvalidOperationException guard permits impossible object operations. Comparing or reporting the wrong clock-out value permits invalid time ranges or produces misleading diagnostics.
summary: Expected business rejection returns a normal result; an operation the object cannot support throws. Session 24 verifies false, InvalidOperationException, and ArgumentOutOfRangeException contracts without reimplementing behavior that already works.
